idiom_name: JPA persistence context (dirty checking + flush) inside a JTA or Spring transaction
implementation_notes: The JPA persistence context is the unit of work: entity instances become managed when they are persisted, found or merged, the provider tracks their loaded state, dirty checking detects modifications, and the state is synchronised to the database on flush or when the associated transaction commits - the Java EE tutorial states plainly that the state of persistent entities is synchronised when the transaction commits. Spring's @Transactional (declarative, rollback rules in configuration) or a JTA UserTransaction defines the boundary; you never keep change lists yourself. Plain JDBC remains the manual base layer: con.setAutoCommit(false) followed by commit/rollback with hand-written tracking, where JDBC savepoints (con.setSavepoint, con.rollback(save)) give partial rollback.
pitfalls: Entity lifecycle mistakes surface at commit: persisting a detached instance throws, and merge() on a detached graph can silently overwrite newer rows.
An extended or over-long persistence context accumulates managed entities and serves stale reads; the context should be scoped to the transaction or request.
EntityManager is not thread-safe, and the same context must not be shared by concurrent threads.
Calling em.flush() to make data visible defeats batching and can deadlock against the transaction's own locks; force a flush only where read-your-writes is required.

variants.name: JDBC auto-commit off with a hand-written change set
variants.idiom_name: Connection.setAutoCommit(false) + PreparedStatement batch + own change list
variants.implementation_notes: Without an ORM the unit of work is explicit JDBC: disable auto-commit on one connection, add every statement to PreparedStatement batches or execute them in order, call commit() and roll back in the catch block, and keep the new/dirty/removed lists yourself. Use it for bulk jobs and statement-oriented code where the persistence context's tracking would only add overhead; savepoints (setSavepoint/rollback(Savepoint)) provide partial rollback inside the unit of work.
pitfalls: Calling rollback() is the only way to know what was committed after a SQLException - a caught exception does not tell you how far the transaction got.
The connection must be released and auto-commit restored; leaking a connection with auto-commit off poisons the pool.
Batch sizes are bounded by the driver and the database (statement limits, lock duration); flushing everything in one batch can exhaust memory or block writers.
